title: Vegetables As Ingredients, Not Punishment
lede: Most people don't hate vegetables — they hate boiled vegetables. Browning, high heat, and a little acid convert the same carrot from a limp obligation into something you actually reach for.

blocks.html: If you think you dislike vegetables, run the audit: nearly every vegetable you remember disliking was boiled or steamed — grey-green, waterlogged, flavour left behind in the pot. That is not the vegetable's fault. It is a processing failure, the culinary equivalent of judging coffee by a scorched gas-station pot.

The whole module rests on one mechanism you already respect from roasting coffee: browning. Above roughly 140 °C the surface of a food stops merely getting hot and starts getting chemically transformed — hundreds of new aroma compounds appear that simply do not exist in the raw or boiled ingredient. Boiling caps out at 100 °C, so no matter how long you wait, that door never opens. Worse, water actively pulls flavour and sugar out of the vegetable and into the pot you then pour down the sink.

So the plan is deliberate: we do not start with salad. Salad asks a raw vegetable to be delicious with no help — a hard mode you earn later. We start where the transformation is largest and the payoff most obvious: roasting, high-heat searing and stir-frying, then a light first pass at pickling and fermenting. By the end, a vegetable is a component you build a meal around, not a tax you pay to feel virtuous.

blocks.label: The one-line thesis
blocks.html: Boiled vegetables taste of nothing because 100 °C is below the temperature at which flavour is created and because water carries flavour away. Every technique in this module is a way to get a dry vegetable surface hotter than 140 °C.

Think of heat as a ladder of unlockable reactions. Each rung switches on a different chemistry. The reason your oven runs at 220 °C and your boiling pot cannot exceed 100 °C is the entire story of this module in one picture.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1 — Boiling lives permanently below the browning line. Roasting and searing put the surface into the caramelisation and Maillard bands, where flavour is manufactured.

blocks.html: Two mechanisms do almost all the work, and they overlap:

• Maillard reaction — amino acids react with reducing sugars on a dry surface above ~140 °C. This is savoury, roasted, complex: the crust on roast potato, the char on a stir-fried green bean.
  • Caramelisation — sugars alone decompose above ~160 °C into sweet, nutty, bitter-edged compounds. This is why sugary vegetables (onion, carrot, pepper, squash) turn candy-sweet when roasted.

The gatekeeper for both is surface moisture. Water on the surface pins the temperature at 100 °C — all incoming heat is spent boiling that water off rather than raising the temperature. Until the surface is dry, nothing browns. This single fact explains every roasting rule below.

items.title: Maillard reaction
items.html: What: amino acids + reducing sugars react on a dry surface >140 °C. Why it matters: it invents savoury, roasted aroma that raw and boiled vegetables lack entirely. Common mistake: a wet surface — it never gets past 100 °C, so it steams grey instead of browning.

items.title: Caramelisation
items.html: What: sugars alone break down >160 °C into sweet/nutty compounds. Why it matters: it is why roasted carrot and onion taste of candy. Common mistake: expecting it fast — real onion caramelisation is 20–40 min, not the 5 min recipes claim.

items.title: Surface moisture = the enemy
items.html: What: water pins the surface at 100 °C until it boils off. Why it matters: drying and spacing is 80% of good roast veg. Common mistake: tossing wet-washed vegetables straight onto the tray.

items.title: Crowding = steaming
items.html: What: pieces packed together trap the water they release as steam. Why it matters: a crowded tray self-boils in its own moisture. Common mistake: #1 beginner error — one heaped tray instead of two spaced ones.

items.title: Cell walls & texture
items.html: What: pectin and cellulose soften with heat; that's what "tender" is. Why it matters: you stop partway for crisp-tender, or go all the way for silky. Common mistake: cooking to one endpoint by habit and calling everything "done".

items.title: Salt & acid make veg crave-able
items.html: What: salt draws water out (osmosis) and seasons; acid brightens and preserves. Why it matters: a squeeze of lemon or a pickled onion can save a dull dish. Common mistake: under-salting, then blaming the vegetable.

blocks.label: Variable that matters most
blocks.html: If you tune only one thing this month, tune surface dryness × pan/tray crowding. Together they decide whether your vegetables brown or stew, and no amount of seasoning fixes a stewed vegetable after the fact.
Vegetable cookery is forgiving on gear. Heat capacity and surface area matter far more than brand.

rows.value: Two heavy rimmed half-sheets. Two so you never crowd — the single most impactful purchase in this module.

To dry washed vegetables. Dry surface > expensive tray, every time.

A small convection oven. Useful, but not magic — it browns because it's a hot, well-ventilated box, the same physics as your oven.
Coatings degrade at high roast temps and grip fond poorly. Bare metal browns better.

blocks.html: Roasting — the default transformation

1. Prep — cut uniform, cut generous. Even sizes cook evenly; edges brown, so more edges = more flavour. Aim ~2–3 cm chunks. Uneven pieces guarantee some burnt, some raw.
  2. Prep — dry ruthlessly. Pat washed vegetables bone-dry with a towel. Every drop of surface water is time and energy stolen from browning (see Fig. 1).
  3. Prep — oil enough for contact, not a swim. ~1 tbsp oil per tray of veg. Oil is the thermal bridge between metal/air and surface; too little = dry spots, too much = fried and greasy.
  4. Execute — hot oven, single layer, space between pieces. 220 °C / 425 °F fan or hotter. One layer, gaps you can see the tray through. Two trays beat one heaped tray every single time.
  5. Execute — leave it alone, then turn once. Contact time builds crust. Flip once at the two-thirds mark; constant fiddling resets the browning clock.
  6. Evaluate — read the colour and the edges. Deep golden-brown edges, a caramel base, tender centre when pierced. Pale = not done regardless of the timer.
  7. Correct — pale after full time? Oven's too cool (check the £8 thermometer) or the tray was crowded. Crank heat for the last 5–8 min or split onto two trays and continue.

rows.value: 2–4 cm chunks · parboil 8–10 min in salted water, drain, dry, rough up in the pan · onto a preheated oiled tray · 45–55 min. Roughed, gelatinised surface = maximum crisp.
Halved lengthways or 3 cm oblique cut · high sugar → caramelises fast · 25–35 min · finish with acid or honey.
2–3 cm strips or halves · high water + high sugar · 25–35 min · roast hot to blister skin before water stews them.
Thick wedges root-attached (they hold together) · 30–40 min for sweet roasted edges — a different process from stovetop caramelising.

blocks.html: Two ways to brown an onion — and why one recipe lies
"Caramelise the onions (5 min)" is the most common lie in recipe writing. There are two distinct processes and they are not interchangeable:

items.title: Quick high-heat char (5–8 min)
items.html: Screaming pan, thin slices, kept moving. You get Maillard char on the edges — savoury, smoky, still sharp and oniony inside. Great in a stir-fry. This is not caramelised onion.

items.title: Low-and-slow caramelisation (20–40+ min)
items.html: Medium-low heat, patience, occasional stir, a splash of water to deglaze. Sugars slowly break down; the onion collapses to jammy, sweet, deep brown. Time is the ingredient — there is no 5-minute shortcut, because sugar chemistry runs at the speed it runs.

blocks.html: Stir-fry & high-heat searing

1. Prep — mise en place, everything dry and cut. Stir-fry is fast; there's no time to chop mid-cook. Wet vegetables drop the pan temperature and steam.
  2. Execute — get the pan screaming first. You want the surface hot enough that the moment food lands it sears, not sweats. A drop of water should skitter and evaporate instantly.
  3. Execute — cook in batches, keep it moving. Overloading crashes the temperature into stewing territory. Small batches keep the metal hot; movement gives every face a flash of char without soft-cooking the interior.
  4. Evaluate — crisp-tender, with char freckles. Bright colour, snap remaining, blistered spots. Cell walls (pectin/cellulose) have softened just enough — stop before the centre goes limp.
  5. Correct — grey and wet, not charred? Pan too cool or batch too big. Remove everything, reheat the pan fully, go again in smaller loads.

blocks.label: Mediocre → Excellent
blocks.html: Mediocre cooks fill the pan and stir constantly at medium heat — they boil vegetables in a skillet. Excellent cooks run the pan hotter than feels comfortable, cook less at once, and accept a few near-black char spots as the flavour, not a mistake.
Salting to draw water (osmosis)

Watery vegetables — cucumber, courgette/zucchini, cabbage — brown badly and dilute dishes. Salt them first: toss with ~1–2% salt by weight, wait 15–30 min, then squeeze or pat dry. Osmosis pulls interior water out through the cell membranes, leaving them firmer, more concentrated, and far more willing to brown or take up a pickle brine.

fields.detail: Crowded tray trapping steam; wet surfaces; oven too cool; too much oil.
Was there space between pieces? Did you dry them? Check real oven temp with a thermometer.
Split across two trays in a single layer, dry the veg, run 220 °C+ fan, and don't flip until a crust has set.

blocks.problem: Pale — cooked through but no colour

fields.detail: Surface never reached ~140 °C: cool oven, crowding, or steam from a covered tray.
Tender inside but blond outside is the signature. Almost always a temperature/steam problem, not time.
Uncover, raise heat to 230 °C for the last 5–10 min, or move to the top of the oven near the element.
Heat too high for the piece size; chunks cut too large; dense veg (potato, squash) not parboiled.
Dark crust with a hard, starchy centre. The surface outran the interior.
Cut smaller and uniform, drop to 200 °C, or parboil dense vegetables first so the oven only has to brown, not cook through.
Pan not hot enough; too much in the pan at once; wet vegetables; constant low-heat stirring.
Pooled liquid in the pan means you're boiling, not frying.
Empty the pan, reheat until smoking-hot, dry the veg, and cook in batches half the size.
High-water vegetables (courgette, mushroom, cabbage) released their water into the dish.
A thin puddle and pale colour at the end of cooking.
Pre-salt to draw water out (osmosis), cook those vegetables separately over high heat, and add them back at the end.

blocks.html: Same principle as calibrating an espresso shot: change one variable, hold the rest, read the result. Do these back-to-back so the comparison is live in your mouth.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E1 — crowded vs spaced

fields.detail: Feel the steaming-vs-browning mechanism directly.
Same vegetable, cut, oil, oven (220 °C fan), time.
Tray A heaped and packed; Tray B single layer with gaps.
A comes out pale and soft; B comes out browned and crisp.
Look for pooled moisture and grey colour on A; caramel edges on B. Taste both.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E2 — dry vs wet surface

fields.detail: Isolate surface moisture as the browning gatekeeper.
Same veg, spacing, oil, oven, time. Both spaced properly.
Batch A patted bone-dry; Batch B left wet from washing.
A browns on schedule; B spends its first 8–12 min drying and finishes paler.
Note how much longer B takes to colour — that lag is water boiling off at 100 °C.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E3 — parboiled & roughed vs raw-cut potato

fields.detail: See why the classic crispy roast potato technique works.
Same potatoes, oil, tray, 220 °C, 50 min.
Batch A parboiled 8–10 min, drained, dried, roughed up in the pan; Batch B cut raw and roasted straight.
A develops a shaggy, gelatinised, ultra-crisp shell; B is smoother and noticeably less crunchy.
The roughed starchy surface area on A is the whole trick — more micro-edges to crisp.

blocks.title: Controlled experiment · E4 — onion at 5 min vs 30 min

fields.detail: Prove that caramelisation is a time process, not a heat shortcut.
Same onion, same slice, same medium-low heat, same pan and fat.
Pull half at 5 min; cook the rest to 30+ min with occasional deglaze.
5-min is soft but still sharp and pale; 30-min is jammy, deep brown, sweet.
Taste side by side. This is why "caramelise in 5 minutes" recipes are lying.
Reliable deep browning with zero stewing.

blocks.label: What beginners get wrong here
blocks.html: They plate a naked roasted vegetable and stop. The advanced move is contrast: something browned, something bright/acidic, something creamy, something crunchy. A pickled onion or a squeeze of lemon is doing structural work, not decoration.

blocks.query: roasted vegetables crowded pan vs spaced out
blocks.look: Look for: the packed tray is pale and glossy-wet; the spaced tray shows caramel-brown edges. This is Fig. 2 in real photos.
Look for: the colour march from translucent → gold → deep brown. Note how far past 5 min real caramelisation is.

blocks.query: crispy roast potatoes rough edges gelatinised surface
blocks.look: Look for: the shaggy, craggy exterior on parboiled-and-roughed potatoes vs the smooth face of raw-cut ones.

blocks.query: wok hei charred stir fry vegetables blistered
blocks.look: Look for: dark char freckles on still-vivid vegetables — seared, not stewed. Colour stays bright.

blocks.html: Knowledge check — understanding, not recall

questions: You steamed broccoli to perfect tenderness. Explain, in terms of temperature, why it still can't taste roasted no matter how long you cook it.
A friend crowds one tray "to save oven space" and gets pale, soft veg. Diagram the mechanism that ruined it, and give two fixes that don't require more oven trays.
Why does patting vegetables dry actually change the temperature the surface can reach, rather than just "helping a bit"?
A recipe says "caramelise the onions, 5 minutes." What will you actually get at 5 minutes, and what has to change for true caramelisation?
Your courgette dish came out watery. Name the mechanism you'd use before cooking to prevent it, and explain why it works.

blocks.label: Practical challenge
blocks.html: Cook the same vegetable two ways in one sitting — boiled/steamed and properly roasted — and taste them side by side. Then execute the L4 project: a vegetable side good enough that a vegetable-sceptic asks for seconds. Photograph the tray before it goes in (check your spacing).

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.html: Write three lines: which single variable moved your results most this month (probably spacing or surface dryness), where you were still stewing without realising, and what "vegetables as an ingredient, not punishment" now means to you in practice. Carry the browning-and-acid instinct into Module 05.
